cls: Vegetable oil (alpha-linolenic acid); vehicle in topical analgesic gels
pharm: Vegetable oil (alpha-linolenic acid); vehicle in topical analgesic gels
quick: Apply a thin layer of the combination gel over the painful area three to four times daily
summary: Linseed (flaxseed) oil is a plant oil rich in alpha-linolenic acid. In India it appears mainly in diclofenac and methyl salicylate topical gels and sprays, where it acts as an emollient vehicle and penetration aid. It is also taken orally as an omega-3 supplement.
indications: Component of topical analgesic gels for musculoskeletal pain (the effect is from the NSAID and rubefacients)
Oral dietary source of alpha-linolenic acid

dosage.d: Apply a thin layer of the combination gel over the painful area three to four times daily
dosage.n: Dose is set by the active NSAID

admin: Wash hands after applying topical gels; avoid eyes and mucosa
moa: Emollient oil; alpha-linolenic acid is a precursor of EPA and DHA with low conversion in humans.
preg: Topical gel: avoid NSAID gels in the third trimester. Oral oil: food amounts are safe
lact: Safety not established; weigh benefit against unknown risk

moderate: Oral high doses: may add to antiplatelet effects

counsel: Use exactly as the pack directs
Stop and seek care for rash, swelling or breathing difficulty
missed: Take it when remembered unless the next dose is due; do not double up.
overdose: No specific antidote. Supportive and symptomatic care.
refs: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health: herbs and supplements
Martindale: The Complete Drug Reference (Pharmaceutical Press)
footer: StewardMD-authored DRAFT. No US, Canadian or EU regulatory label exists for this molecule; AI-drafted from the references above and awaiting clinician review. Doses are typical published ranges, not a product label: check the Indian product's own pack insert before prescribing.
